dublinCore.title: Noise Analysis and Reduction Tool
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Random signals
Noise
Power spectral density
Signal-to-noise ratio
Noise reduction
dublinCore.description: Generates white Gaussian, white uniform, pink (1/f), brown (1/f^2), band-limited and impulsive noise; shows its time series, histogram with a Gaussian fit, autocorrelation and log-log Welch PSD with a fitted slope; and measures the SNR of a 5 Hz sinusoid before and after ensemble averaging and a moving-average or median filter.
relation: Chapter 12: Stochastic Processes and Random Signals

learningObjectives: Classify a noise record as white, pink or brown from its measured PSD slope (0, -10 or -20 dB/decade) and its autocorrelation
Distinguish Gaussian, uniform and impulsive white noise using the histogram and the excess kurtosis, even though their spectra are identical
Explain the variance-resolution trade-off of Welch's method in terms of the number of segments S and the segment length M

Predict the SNR gain of averaging K independent realizations (10 log10 K) and of an L-point moving average on white noise (10 log10 L), and explain why a moving average gains little against pink or brown noise
Evaluate when a moving-average or median filter improves the output SNR, accounting for signal distortion at long L and for impulsive noise
prerequisites: Mean, variance and the Gaussian distribution
Decibels and the definition of SNR
Discrete Fourier transform and power spectral density

misconceptions.misconception: Averaging L samples always improves the SNR by 10 log10 L dB
misconceptions.correction: The 10 log10 L gain needs uncorrelated noise samples; averaging independent realizations gives 10 log10 K for any noise colour
misconceptions.evidence: A 16-point moving average gains 11.95 dB on white noise but only 1.83 dB on pink and 0.01 dB on brown noise, while averaging 16 realizations gains about 12 dB for every colour

misconceptions.correction: Whiteness describes the spectrum and autocorrelation; Gaussianity describes the amplitude distribution
misconceptions.evidence: White uniform and impulsive noise have flat PSDs and rho[1] near 0, but excess kurtosis of -1.20 and +45.4 instead of 0

accessibility.screenReaderScript: Noise analysis tool with four plots: the noisy time series with the clean 5 Hz sinusoid and the averaged output, a histogram with a Gaussian fit, the autocorrelation, and a log-log Welch power spectral density with a fitted slope. A banner reports input SNR, the SNR gain of ensemble averaging and of a moving-average or median filter, and the output SNR.

controls.label: Samples N
controls.description: Record length in samples at fs = 1 kHz

controls.label: New noise
controls.description: Draws a new set of noise realizations (the random seed advances by one)

controls.label: Noise RMS σ
controls.description: Standard deviation of the noise; the sinusoid amplitude scales with it so the input SNR is unchanged

controls.label: Welch segments S
controls.description: Number of Hann-windowed segments averaged in the PSD estimate; the segment length M is the largest power of two with (S+1)M/2 <= N

controls.label: Add 5 Hz sinusoid
controls.description: Adds the test sinusoid s[n] so that SNR can be measured

controls.label: Input SNR
controls.description: Sets the sinusoid amplitude A = sigma * sqrt(2 * 10^(SNR/10))

controls.label: Ensemble avg K
controls.description: Number of independent noisy copies averaged before filtering

controls.label: Filter
controls.description: Chooses a centred moving-average or running-median filter

controls.label: Filter length L
controls.description: Window length of the moving-average or median filter (L = 1 means no filtering)

visualElements.description: Banner: input SNR (or noise power), ensemble-average gain with 10 log10 K, filter gain with the white-noise value 10 log10 L, output SNR and the correlation of output and clean signal
Time series of the first 1.02 s: input x = s + w (blue), clean sinusoid (dashed) and output y (orange)
Histogram of the input noise with a Gaussian of the same mean and variance, the output-noise histogram, and mean, variance and excess kurtosis read-outs
Autocorrelation of the input and output noise for lags 0-100 with the theoretical curve and the 95% band for white noise
Log-log Welch PSD of input and output with the theoretical noise PSD and a fitted slope in dB/decade

model.description: Seeded noise generators produce K independent realizations w_k[n] at fs = 1 kHz. The sketch adds s[n] = A sin(2 pi 5 n / fs), averages the K noisy copies, applies a centred moving-average or median filter of length L, and measures every stage against the clean sinusoid.
equations: ensemble gain (white or not) = 10 log10 K
moving-average gain on white noise = 10 log10 L
white PSD = 2 sigma^2 / fs (one-sided); pink ~ 1/f (-10 dB/decade); brown ~ 1/f^2 (-20 dB/decade)
band-limited autocorrelation = sinc with zeros at multiples of 1/(2B) = 10 ms
algorithms: Mulberry32 seeded uniform generator and Box-Muller Gaussian transform
Pink noise: Paul Kellet's parallel bank of six one-pole filters
Brown noise: leaky integrator with pole 0.999
Band-limited noise: ideal FFT low-pass at 50 Hz
Impulsive noise: Bernoulli-Gaussian, 5% spikes plus a weak Gaussian background
Welch PSD with Hann windows and a radix-2 FFT
Weighted least-squares fit of 10 log10 PSD against log10 f (bins weighted 1/k)
Running median with a sorted window
limitations: A single realization's PSD slope typically differs from theory by 1-2 dB/decade
Pink and brown realizations vary strongly in power, so their measured gains fluctuate around the theoretical values
The filters are centred (zero-phase) and their outputs exist only where the whole window fits

instructionalStrategies: Fingerprint table: record slope, rho[1] and kurtosis for each noise type
Predict-then-measure SNR gains for K and L
Compare linear and nonlinear filters on Gaussian and impulsive noise
extensions: Add a Wiener filter using the known signal and noise PSDs
Replace the sinusoid with a pulse or speech-like test signal
